## How To Use This Page

This page is designed to stand in for slides. Every data story type below has several **candidate visuals**. Each candidate is numbered, captioned, and shows the code that produced it, so you can pick the ones that best fit your lecture and your audience.

Every example uses Seaborn and Matplotlib. Wherever possible the data come from Seaborn's built-in example datasets. Where no built-in dataset makes the point (review summaries, dials, a battery gauge), the data are fictional and are generated in plain sight in the code.

| Story type | The question it answers | Typical visuals |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Comparison | How do groups differ? | Side-by-side box or violin plots, bar charts |
| Change over time | What happened, and when? | Line charts, one violin per year |
| Correlation | Do two things move together? | Scatter, hexbin, heat map |
| Distribution | What does one variable look like? | Histogram, solo box, solo violin |
| Composition | What are the parts of the whole? | Pie, stacked bar, 100% stacked bar |
| Ranking | Who or what is best, and who is worst? | Leader boards, review summaries |
| Process or status | Where are we right now? | Dials, meters, Sankey, battery |

### Setup

All figures share the same imports and the same Seaborn context.

```{python}
#| label: setup

# Import Pandas, Seaborn, and related
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Set the Seaborn context
sns.set_context('talk')
```

# The Comparison Stories

A comparison story answers the question *how do these groups differ?* The reader should be able to see, in a glance, which group is higher, lower, or more spread out. Side-by-side box plots and violin plots show the whole distribution for each group. Bar charts reduce each group to a single number, which is simpler but hides spread.

Candidates: @fig-cmp-box, @fig-cmp-violin, @fig-cmp-bar, @fig-cmp-grouped-bar.

```{python}
#| label: cmp-data

# Load the example datasets used in this section
penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins')
tips = sns.load_dataset('tips')
mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')
titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
```

## Candidate 1: Side-by-Side Box Plots

A box plot reduces each group to five numbers (minimum, quartiles, median, maximum) and flags outliers. It is the quickest way to compare centers and spreads.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cmp-box
#| fig-cap: "Side-by-side box plots compare penguin body mass across three species. The label on each box is the species median."

# Compute the median body mass of each species
medians = penguins.groupby('species')['body_mass_g'].median()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Box plot of body mass by species
sns.boxplot(data=penguins, x='species', y='body_mass_g',
            order=medians.index, hue='species',
            palette='pastel', legend=False, ax=ax)

# Label the median of each box
for i, m in enumerate(medians):
    ax.text(i, m, '{:,.0f} g'.format(m),
            ha='center', va='center', size='xx-small',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.8))

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Gentoo Penguins Are Heavier Than Others')
ax.set_xlabel('Penguin Species')
ax.set_ylabel('Body Mass (grams)')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Side-by-Side Violin Plots

A violin plot adds the *shape* of each distribution. The inner box keeps the familiar quartile summary while the outline reveals skew and multiple peaks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cmp-violin
#| fig-cap: "Side-by-side violin plots compare restaurant bill totals by day of the week. The inner boxes show quartiles and the labels at the top show each day's mean."

# Compute the mean bill for each day
mean_bill = tips.groupby('day', observed=True)['total_bill'].mean()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Violin plot of total bill by day
sns.violinplot(data=tips, x='day', y='total_bill',
               order=mean_bill.index, hue='day', inner='box',
               palette='pastel', legend=False, ax=ax)

# Label the mean of each violin along the top
for i, m in enumerate(mean_bill):
    ax.text(i, 58, 'Mean\n${:.2f}'.format(m),
            ha='center', va='center', size='small')

# Make room for the labels
ax.set_ylim(0, 65)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Weekend Bills Are Larger Than Weekday Bills')
ax.set_xlabel('Day of the Week')
ax.set_ylabel('Total (Dollars)')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Bar Chart of Group Averages

When the audience only needs the headline number, a bar chart with height labels is the clearest choice. Remember that the bars hide the spread within each group.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cmp-bar
#| fig-cap: "A bar chart with height labels compares average fuel efficiency by region of vehicle origin."

# Compute the average miles per gallon by origin
avg_mpg = mpg.groupby('origin')['mpg'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Bar chart of average mpg by origin
sns.barplot(x=avg_mpg.index.str.title(), y=avg_mpg.values,
            hue=avg_mpg.index.str.title(), palette='pastel',
            legend=False, ax=ax)

# Add height labels above the bars
for i, v in enumerate(avg_mpg):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.5, '{:.1f}'.format(v),
            ha='center', size='x-large')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Japanese Cars Lead in Fuel Efficiency')
ax.set_xlabel('Region of Vehicle Origin')
ax.set_ylabel('Average (MPG)')
ax.set_ylim(0, 36)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 4: Grouped Bar Chart

A grouped bar chart compares groups across a second categorical variable. Keep the number of bars manageable so each height label stays readable.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cmp-grouped-bar
#| fig-cap: "A grouped bar chart compares the Titanic survival rate of women and men within each passenger class."

# Compute the survival rate (as a percent) by class and sex
survival = (titanic.groupby(['pclass', 'sex'])['survived']
            .mean().mul(100).reset_index())

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

# Grouped bar chart of survival rate
sns.barplot(data=survival, x='pclass', y='survived',
            hue='sex', palette='pastel', ax=ax)

# Add height labels above each bar
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt='%.0f%%', padding=3, size='medium')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Women Survived at Higher Rates Than Men')
ax.set_xlabel('Passenger Class')
ax.set_ylabel('Survival Rate (%)')
ax.set_ylim(0, 110)
ax.legend(loc='upper right')

plt.show()
```

# The Change Over Time Stories

A change over time story answers *what happened, and when?* Time goes on the horizontal axis and the eye follows the line. Line charts are the default. When the audience needs to see how the whole distribution shifted, one violin or box plot per period works well.

Candidates: @fig-time-annual, @fig-time-multiline, @fig-time-annotated, @fig-time-ci, @fig-time-violin, @fig-time-seasonal.

```{python}
#| label: time-data

# Load the example datasets used in this section
flights = sns.load_dataset('flights')
health = sns.load_dataset('healthexp')
dowjones = sns.load_dataset('dowjones')
fmri = sns.load_dataset('fmri')
mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')
```

## Candidate 1: Simple Line Chart With Point Labels

One series, one story. Markers and data labels let the audience read exact values without hunting for gridlines.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-annual
#| fig-cap: "A line chart with data labels shows total airline passengers (in thousands) for each year from 1949 to 1960."

# Total the monthly passengers into an annual figure
annual = flights.groupby('year')['passengers'].sum().reset_index()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Line chart of annual passengers
sns.lineplot(data=annual, x='year', y='passengers',
             marker='o', markersize=9, ax=ax)

# Label each point
for _, row in list(annual.iterrows())[1::3]:
    ax.text(row['year'], row['passengers'] + 350,
            '{:,.0f}'.format(row['passengers']),
            ha='center', size='x-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Air Travel Grew Rapidly From 1949 To 1960')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Total Passengers (thousands)')
ax.set_xticks(annual['year'])
ax.set_xticklabels(annual['year'], rotation=45)
ax.set_ylim(0, 6600)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Multiple Lines With Direct Labels

Labeling the end of each line removes the need to match colors against a legend, which is much easier to follow on a projector.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-multiline
#| fig-cap: "A multi-line chart with direct labels at the end of each line tracks life expectancy in three countries from 1970 to 2020."

# Assign one color to each country
health = health[health['Country'].isin(['Japan','Germany','USA'])]
countries = health['Country'].unique()
palette = dict(zip(countries, sns.color_palette('tab10', len(countries))))

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

# One line per country
sns.lineplot(data=health, x='Year', y='Life_Expectancy',
             hue='Country', palette=palette, linewidth=3,
             legend=False, ax=ax)

# Label the end of each line
for country, group in health.groupby('Country'):
    last = group.loc[group['Year'].idxmax()]
    ax.text(last['Year'] + 0.7, last['Life_Expectancy'], country,
            color=palette[country], va='center', size='small')

# Make room for the labels
ax.set_xlim(1970, 2032)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Japan Pulled Ahead on Life Expectancy')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Life Expectancy (years)')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Annotated Line Chart

An annotation turns a line into a story by pointing at the moment that matters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-annotated
#| fig-cap: "An annotated line chart shows the monthly Dow Jones average from 1914 to 1968 with the 1929 peak and the 1932 low marked."

# Find the 1929 peak and the low that followed
early = dowjones[dowjones['Date'] < '1940-01-01']
peak = early.loc[early['Price'].idxmax()]
after = early[early['Date'] > peak['Date']]
low = after.loc[after['Price'].idxmin()]

# Find the first month the average climbed back to the peak
recovery = dowjones[(dowjones['Date'] > low['Date']) &
                    (dowjones['Price'] >= peak['Price'])].iloc[0]

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

# Line chart of the Dow Jones average
sns.lineplot(data=dowjones, x='Date', y='Price', ax=ax)

# Annotate the peak, the low, and the recovery
ax.annotate('Sep 1929 peak: {:.0f}'.format(peak['Price']),
            xy=(peak['Date'], peak['Price']),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp('1916-01-01'), 600),
            arrowprops={'arrowstyle': '->'}, size='xx-small')
ax.annotate('1932 low: {:.0f}'.format(low['Price']),
            xy=(low['Date'], low['Price']),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp('1933-01-01'),325),
            arrowprops={'arrowstyle': '->'}, size='xx-small')
ax.annotate('Recovered in {}'.format(recovery['Date'].year),
            xy=(recovery['Date'], recovery['Price']),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp('1938-01-01'), 700),
            arrowprops={'arrowstyle': '->'}, size='xx-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Dow Took 25 Yrs to Recover From 1929 Crash')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Dow Jones Average')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 4: Line Chart With Uncertainty Bands

When each time point is built from many measurements, Seaborn automatically averages them and shades a 95% confidence interval.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-ci
#| fig-cap: "A line chart with shaded 95% confidence bands shows the average brain signal at each timepoint for two kinds of event."

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Line chart with confidence band, one line per event type
sns.lineplot(data=fmri, x='timepoint', y='signal',
             hue='event', style='event', markers=True,
             linewidth=3, ax=ax)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Stimulation Responses Vs Cue Responses')
ax.set_xlabel('Timepoint')
ax.set_ylabel('Average Signal')
ax.legend(title='Event')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 5: One Violin Per Year

When a line of averages would hide how the whole distribution moved, draw one violin per period. The line over the violins carries the median.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-violin
#| fig-cap: "One violin per model year shows the distribution of fuel efficiency from 1970 to 1982. The line connects the yearly medians."

# Compute the median mpg for each model year
yearly_median = mpg.groupby('model_year')['mpg'].median()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

# One violin per model year
sns.violinplot(data=mpg, x='model_year', y='mpg', ax=ax)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Fuel Efficiency Jumped After 1979')
ax.set_xlabel('Model Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Fuel Efficiency (MPG)')
ax.set_xticks(range(len(yearly_median)))
ax.set_xticklabels(['19{}'.format(y) for y in yearly_median.index], rotation=45)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 6: One Line Per Year to Reveal Seasonality

Drawing each year as its own line, with a sequential color scale, reveals a repeating pattern and shows whether it is growing.

```{python}
#| label: fig-time-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "One line per year, shaded from light to dark, shows monthly airline passengers and the repeating summer peak."

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3))

# One line per year, colored on a sequential palette
sns.lineplot(data=flights, x='month', y='passengers',
             hue='year', palette='viridis', linewidth=2.5, ax=ax)

# Move the legend outside the graph area
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc=2, borderaxespad=0.,
          title='Year', fontsize='xx-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Yearly Patterns Repeat')
ax.set_xlabel('Month')
ax.set_ylabel('Passengers')

# Shrink the x-axis labels so the month names fit
ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize='x-small', rotation=45)

plt.show()
```

# The Correlation Stories

A correlation story answers *do these two things move together?* Scatter plots show the raw relationship between two numeric variables. When there are too many points, hexbin plots show density instead. When both variables are categorical, cross-tabulate them and show the table as a heat map.

Candidates: @fig-corr-reg, @fig-corr-simpson, @fig-corr-hexbin, @fig-corr-heat, @fig-corr-crosstab, @fig-corr-bubble.

```{python}
#| label: corr-data

# Load the example datasets used in this section
mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')
penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins')
diamonds = sns.load_dataset('diamonds')
titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
crashes = sns.load_dataset('car_crashes')
```

## Candidate 1: Scatter Plot With Trend Line

The classic correlation visual. The trend line and the correlation coefficient give the audience a number to remember.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-reg
#| fig-cap: "A scatter plot with a fitted trend line shows vehicle weight against fuel efficiency. The correlation coefficient is printed in the corner."

# Compute the correlation between weight and mpg
r = mpg['weight'].corr(mpg['mpg'])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Scatter plot with a regression line
sns.regplot(data=mpg, x='weight', y='mpg',
            scatter_kws={'s': 15, 'alpha': 0.6},
            line_kws={'color': 'darkred'}, ax=ax)

# Print the correlation coefficient in the corner
ax.text(0.95, 0.95, 'r = {:.2f}'.format(r),
        transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='top', size='small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Heavier Cars Are Less Efficient')
ax.set_xlabel('Vehicle Weight (lbs)')
ax.set_ylabel('Fuel Efficiency (MPG)')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Scatter Plot That Reverses Within Groups

Color the points by a third variable to show that a correlation can change direction once the groups are separated (Simpson's paradox). The dashed line is the overall trend.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-simpson
#| fig-cap: "A scatter plot of penguin bill length and bill depth, colored by species. The dashed line is the overall trend, which slopes down, while the trend inside each species slopes up."

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Scatter plot colored by species
sns.scatterplot(data=penguins, x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm',
                hue='species', style='species', ax=ax)

# Overall trend line that ignores species
sns.regplot(data=penguins, x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm',
            scatter=False, color='black',
            line_kws={'linestyle': '--'}, ax=ax)

# Move the legend into an empty corner
ax.legend(loc='lower left', fontsize='xx-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Overall Trend Reverses Within Species')
ax.set_xlabel('Bill Length (mm)')
ax.set_ylabel('Bill Depth (mm)')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Hexbin Plot For Crowded Scatter Plots

With tens of thousands of points a scatter plot becomes a solid blob. A hexbin plot counts the points in each hexagon so the density shows through.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-hexbin
#| fig-cap: "Two views of the same 54,000 diamonds. The scatter plot on the left is overplotted, while the hexbin plot on the right shows where the diamonds are concentrated."

# Create a pair of side-by-side axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=2, figsize=(6, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)

# Left: plain scatter plot
sns.scatterplot(data=diamonds, x='carat', y='price',
                s=5, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('Scatter: Overplotted', fontsize='x-small')

# Right: hexbin plot with a log-scaled color bar
hb = axes[1].hexbin(diamonds['carat'], diamonds['price'],
                    gridsize=30, cmap='Blues', mincnt=1, bins='log')
fig.colorbar(hb, ax=axes[1], label='log10(Diamonds)')
axes[1].set_title('Hexbin: Shows Density', fontsize='x-small')

# Set the axis labels
axes[0].set_xlabel('Carat', fontsize='x-small')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Carat', fontsize='x-small')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Price (US dollars)', fontsize='x-small')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 4: Correlation Matrix Heat Map

A heat map of correlation coefficients shows many relationships at once. Masking the upper triangle removes the duplicated half.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-heat
#| fig-cap: "A correlation matrix heat map for six vehicle measurements. Red cells are positive correlations, blue cells are negative, and the upper triangle is hidden because it repeats the lower triangle."

# Compute the correlation matrix
cols = ['mpg', 'cylinders', 'displacement',
        'horsepower', 'weight', 'acceleration']
corr = mpg[cols].corr()

# Hide the upper triangle
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool), k=1)

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Heat map with the coefficients printed in each cell
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt='.2f',
            cmap='coolwarm', vmin=-1, vmax=1, cbar=False,
            annot_kws={'size': 11}, ax=ax)

# Set the title and tick labels
ax.set_title('Heavy Cars Have Low MPG')
ax.tick_params(axis='both', labelsize='x-small')
ax.set_xticklabels(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 5: Cross-Tabulation Heat Map For Categories

When both variables are categorical, count (or take percentages of) every combination with a cross-tabulation, then color the table.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-crosstab
#| fig-cap: "A heat map of a cross-tabulation shows the percent of each port's Titanic passengers in each passenger class. Each column sums to 100%."

# Cross-tabulate class by port, as a percent of each port
ct = pd.crosstab(titanic['class'], titanic['embark_town'],
                 normalize='columns').mul(100)
ct = ct.reindex(['First', 'Second', 'Third'])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Build text labels that end with a percent sign
pct_labels = ct.round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + '%'

# Heat map with the percents printed in each cell
sns.heatmap(ct, annot=pct_labels, fmt='', cmap='Blues',
            cbar=False, annot_kws={'size': 16}, ax=ax)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Class By Embarkation Point')
ax.set_xlabel('Port of Embarkation (% of port)')
ax.set_ylabel('Passenger Class')
ax.tick_params(axis='both', labelsize='x-small')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 6: Bubble Chart

A third numeric variable can ride along as the size of each point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-bubble
#| fig-cap: "A bubble chart plots each US state's alcohol-impaired fatal crash rate against its total fatal crash rate (drivers involved in fatal collisions, per billion vehicle miles traveled). Bubble size shows the rate of fatal crashes involving speeding."

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Bubble chart with speeding as the bubble size
sns.scatterplot(data=crashes, x='alcohol', y='total',
                size='speeding', sizes=(20, 300), alpha=0.5,
                edgecolor='k', legend='brief', ax=ax)

# Shrink the legend and place it in an empty corner
sns.move_legend(ax, 'lower right', fontsize='xx-small',
                title='Speeding', title_fontsize='xx-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('More Alcohol, More Fatal Crashes')
ax.set_xlabel('Alcohol-Impaired Crashes (per billion miles)', fontsize='x-small')
ax.set_ylabel('Fatal Crashes (per bil miles)', fontsize='x-small')
ax.xaxis.label.set_size('small')
ax.yaxis.label.set_size('small')

plt.show()
```

# The Distribution Stories

A distribution story answers *what does this one variable look like?* Where is the center, how wide is the spread, is it skewed, does it have more than one peak? Histograms, solo box plots, and solo violin plots are the workhorses.

Candidates: @fig-dist-hist, @fig-dist-bins, @fig-dist-box, @fig-dist-violin, @fig-dist-ecdf, @fig-dist-bimodal.

```{python}
#| label: dist-data

# Load the example datasets used in this section
diamonds = sns.load_dataset('diamonds')
tips = sns.load_dataset('tips')
titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
geyser = sns.load_dataset('geyser')
```

## Candidate 1: Histogram With Mean And Median

When a distribution is skewed, the mean and the median disagree. Marking both lines makes the skew visible.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-hist
#| fig-cap: "A histogram with a density curve shows the distribution of diamond prices. The dotted line marks the mean and the dashed line marks the median."

# Compute the mean and median price
mean_price = diamonds['price'].mean()
median_price = diamonds['price'].median()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Histogram with a density curve
sns.histplot(data=diamonds, x='price', bins=40, kde=True, ax=ax)

# Mark the median and the mean
# ax.axvline(median_price, color='darkred', linestyle='--',
#            label='Median: ${:,.0f}'.format(median_price))
# ax.axvline(mean_price, color='black', linestyle=':',
#            label='Mean: ${:,.0f}'.format(mean_price))
# ax.legend(fontsize='x-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Diamond Prices Skew Right')
ax.set_xlabel('Price (US dollars)')
ax.set_ylabel('Number of Diamonds')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Same Data, Different Bin Counts

The number of bins is a choice, and the choice changes the story. This is a good figure for teaching that point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-bins
#| fig-cap: "Three histograms of the same restaurant bills drawn with 5, 15, and 40 bins."

# Three bin counts to compare
bin_counts = [5, 15, 40]

# Create a row of three axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=3, figsize=(6, 9))

# Draw the same histogram with a different number of bins in each
for ax, b in zip(axes, bin_counts):
    sns.histplot(data=tips, x='total_bill', bins=b, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title('{} Bins'.format(b))
    ax.set_xlabel('Bill (dollars)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Number of Bills')

# Label the shared y axis once
fig.suptitle('Bin Count Changes What You See', y=1.03)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Solo Box Plot With Labeled Quartiles

A single box plot with the key values printed on it lets the audience read the numbers instead of estimating them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-box
#| fig-cap: "A single horizontal box plot of restaurant bills with the first quartile, median, and third quartile labeled."

# Compute the quartiles
q1, med, q3 = tips['total_bill'].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Single horizontal box plot
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x='total_bill', width=0.4,
            color=sns.color_palette('pastel')[0], ax=ax)

# Label each quartile below the box
# for label, val in [('Q1', q1), ('Median', med), ('Q3', q3)]:
for val in [q1, med, q3]:
    ax.text(val*.85, 0.2, '${:.2f}'.format(val),
            transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(),
            ha='center', va='center', size='xx-small',
            rotation=45)

for val, label in zip([q1, med, q3], ['25th Pctl', '50th Pctl', '75th Pctl']):
    ax.text(val*.95, .83, label,
            transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(),
            ha='left', va='center', size='xx-small',
            rotation=45)

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Half Of Bills Between ${:.0f} - ${:.0f}'.format(q1, q3))
ax.set_xlabel('Total Bill (dollars)')
ax.set_yticks([])

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 4: Solo Violin Plot

A single violin shows the shape that a single box plot hides. Here the quartiles are drawn inside the violin and printed beside it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-violin
#| fig-cap: "A single violin plot of passenger ages on the Titanic with the quartiles labeled."

# Compute the quartiles
q1, med, q3 = titanic['age'].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))

# Single violin plot, trimmed so ages stop at the data
sns.violinplot(data=titanic, y='age', inner='quart', cut=0,
               color=sns.color_palette('pastel')[0], ax=ax)

# Label each quartile beside the violin
for label, val in [('Q3', q3), ('Median', med), ('Q1', q1)]:
    ax.text(0.45, val, '{}: {:.0f}'.format(label, val),
            va='center', size='small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Half Of Passengers Were {:.0f} To {:.0f}'.format(q1, q3))
ax.set_ylabel('Age (years)')
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.1)
ax.set_xticks([])

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 5: Cumulative Distribution

An ECDF answers "what share of the data falls below this value?" directly. It is a favorite when the audience needs to read percentiles.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-ecdf

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

# Empirical cumulative distribution

# Mark the median
ax.axhline(0.5, color='gray', linestyle=':')
ax.axvline(median_bill, color='gray', linestyle=':')
ax.text(median_bill + 1, 0.35, '50% of bills are\nunder ${:.2f}'.format(median_bill),
        size='x-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Half Of Bills Are Under ${:.2f}'.format(median_bill))
ax.set_xlabel('Total Bill (dollars)')
ax.set_ylabel('Share Of Bills')

plt.show()
```

# The Composition Stories

A composition story answers *what are the parts of the whole?* Pie and donut charts work when there are only a few parts and the audience needs a rough share. Stacked bars show composition across several groups, and proportional (100%) stacked bars make the shares comparable even when the group sizes differ.

Candidates: @fig-comp-pie, @fig-comp-donut, @fig-comp-stacked, @fig-comp-prop, @fig-comp-prop-h, @fig-comp-waffle.

```{python}
#| label: comp-data

# Import the patch class used for the waffle chart legend
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

# Load the example datasets used in this section
titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins')
mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')

# Pastel colors shared by every chart in this section
colors = sns.color_palette('pastel')
```

## Candidate 1: Pie Chart

Use a pie chart only when there are a few slices and the point is a rough share of the whole. Percent labels on the slices keep the audience from guessing.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-pie
#| fig-cap: "A pie chart shows the share of Titanic passengers in each passenger class."

# Count the passengers in each class
class_counts = titanic['class'].value_counts()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))

# Pie chart with percent labels
ax.pie(class_counts, labels=class_counts.index.astype(str),
       autopct='%1.0f%%', startangle=90, counterclock=False,
       colors=colors, wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'white'},
       textprops={'size': 'small'})

# Set the title
ax.set_title('Most Passengers Rode Third Class')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Donut Chart

A donut chart is a pie chart with the middle removed. The hole is a convenient place to print the total.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-donut
#| fig-cap: "A donut chart shows the share of penguins in each species. The total number of penguins is printed in the center."

# Count the penguins of each species
species_counts = penguins['species'].value_counts()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))

# Donut chart: a pie with a narrow ring width
ax.pie(species_counts, labels=species_counts.index,
       autopct='%1.0f%%', startangle=90, counterclock=False,
       colors=colors, pctdistance=0.8,
       wedgeprops={'width': 0.4, 'edgecolor': 'white'},
       textprops={'size': 'small'})

# Print the total in the center
ax.text(0, 0, 'n = {}'.format(species_counts.sum()),
        ha='center', va='center', size='large')

# Set the title
ax.set_title('Adelie Is The Largest Species Share')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Stacked Bar Chart

A stacked bar chart shows both the total for each group and how each total breaks down. Label the segments and the totals.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-stacked
#| fig-cap: "A stacked bar chart shows the number of penguins of each species on each island. Segment labels show counts and the number above each bar is the island total."

# Cross-tabulate island by species
ct = pd.crosstab(penguins['island'], penguins['species'])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Stacked bar chart
ct.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, color=colors[:3], rot=0, ax=ax)

# Label each segment, leaving empty segments blank
for container in ax.containers:
    labels = ['' if v == 0 else str(int(v)) for v in container.datavalues]
    ax.bar_label(container, labels=labels, label_type='center', size='small')

# Label the total above each bar
for i, total in enumerate(ct.sum(axis=1)):
    ax.text(i, total + 4, str(total), ha='center', size='small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Only Adelie Live On Torgersen')
ax.set_xlabel('Island')
ax.set_ylabel('Number of Penguins')
ax.set_ylim(0, 190)
ax.legend(title='Species', fontsize='x-small', title_fontsize='x-small')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 4: Proportional Stacked Bar Chart

When group sizes differ, converting every bar to 100% makes the shares directly comparable.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-prop
#| fig-cap: "A proportional stacked bar chart shows the percent of Titanic passengers in each class who survived and who did not."

# Cross-tabulate class by outcome, as a percent of each class
ct = pd.crosstab(titanic['class'], titanic['alive'], normalize='index').mul(100)
ct = ct.rename(columns={'yes': 'Survived', 'no': 'Did Not Survive'})
ct = ct[['Survived', 'Did Not Survive']]

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Proportional stacked bar chart
ct.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, color=colors[:2], rot=0, ax=ax)

# Label each segment with its percent
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt='%.0f%%', label_type='center', size='small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('First Class Survived Most Often')
ax.set_xlabel('Passenger Class')
ax.set_ylabel('Share of Passengers (%)')
ax.legend(loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.25),
          ncol=2, fontsize='x-small')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 5: Horizontal Proportional Stacked Bar Chart

Horizontal bars leave room for long group names and many segments. Hiding the labels on the tiniest segments keeps the chart readable.

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-prop-h
#| fig-cap: "A horizontal proportional stacked bar chart shows the percent of cars from each region of origin by number of engine cylinders. Segments under 6% are not labeled."

# Cross-tabulate origin by cylinders, as a percent of each origin
ct = pd.crosstab(mpg['origin'], mpg['cylinders'], normalize='index').mul(100)
ct.index = ct.index.str.title()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Horizontal proportional stacked bar chart
ct.plot(kind='barh', stacked=True, color=colors[:5], ax=ax)

# Label each large segment with its percent
for container in ax.containers:
    labels = ['{:.0f}%'.format(v) if v >= 6 else '' for v in container.datavalues]
    ax.bar_label(container, labels=labels, label_type='center', size='x-small')

# Put the first group at the top
ax.invert_yaxis()

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('US Cars Use Bigger Engines')
ax.set_xlabel('Share of Cars (%)')
ax.set_ylabel('')
ax.legend(title='Cylinders', loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.25),
          ncol=5, fontsize='x-small', title_fontsize='x-small')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 6: Waffle Chart

A waffle chart is a pie chart you can count. Each square is one percent of the whole, which makes it easy to say "about 4 in 10."

```{python}
#| label: fig-comp-waffle
#| fig-cap: "A waffle chart where each square is one percent of Titanic passengers. The blue squares are the passengers who survived."

# Compute the percent of passengers who survived, rounded to a whole number
survived_pct = int(round(titanic['survived'].mean() * 100))

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Draw a 10 by 10 grid of squares, filling from the top left
for i in range(100):
    row, col = divmod(i, 10)
    color = colors[0] if i < survived_pct else 'lightgray'
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((col, 9 - row), 0.9, 0.9, color=color))

# Tidy the axes
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.axis('off')

# Add a legend and title
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=colors[0], label='Survived'),
                   Patch(color='lightgray', label='Did Not Survive')],
          loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0), ncol=2,
          fontsize='x-small')
ax.set_title('About {} In 10 Passengers Survived'.format(round(survived_pct / 10)))

plt.show()
```

# The Ranking Stories

A ranking story answers *who or what is best, and who or what is worst?* Think of the review summary on a shopping website, a board game leader board, or a list of the most efficient machines. Sort the items, make the order obvious, and label the values.

Candidates: @fig-rank-reviews, @fig-rank-products, @fig-rank-game, @fig-rank-efficient, @fig-rank-lollipop, @fig-rank-bump.

## Candidate 1: Customer Review Summary

This is the star summary found on shopping websites. The data are fictional.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rank-reviews
#| fig-cap: "A customer review summary for a fictional product. Each bar is the share of reviews at that star level, labeled with the percent and the number of reviews."

# Fictional counts of reviews at each star level
stars = pd.DataFrame({
    'rating': [5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
    'reviews': [612, 301, 118, 54, 41]})

# Build a row of solid star characters for each rating
stars['label'] = ['\u2605' * r for r in stars['rating']]

# Compute the share of reviews and the average rating
stars['pct'] = stars['reviews'] / stars['reviews'].sum() * 100
avg_rating = (stars['rating'] * stars['reviews']).sum() / stars['reviews'].sum()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Horizontal bars for each star level
sns.barplot(data=stars, x='pct', y='label', orient='h',
            color='#f4b400', ax=ax)

# Label each bar with its percent and count
for i, row in stars.iterrows():
    ax.text(row['pct'] + 1.5, i,
            '{:.0f}% ({:,})'.format(row['pct'], row['reviews']),
            va='center', size='x-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('{:.1f} Out Of 5 Stars ({:,} Reviews)'.format(
    avg_rating, stars['reviews'].sum()))
ax.set_xlabel('Share of Reviews (%)')
ax.set_ylabel('')
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)

# Color the stars gold
for tick_label in ax.get_yticklabels():
    tick_label.set_color('#f4b400')
sns.despine()

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Rating Comparison Across Products

Pair each rating with the number of reviews behind it so the audience can judge how much to trust it. The data are fictional.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rank-products
#| fig-cap: "Fictional camping products ranked by average star rating. Each label shows the rating and the number of reviews."

# Fictional average ratings and review counts
products = pd.DataFrame({
    'product': ['TrailMix Pro', 'AquaBottle 2', 'PeakPack 30L',
                'SummitStove', 'CampLite Lantern', 'HikeMate Poles'],
    'rating': [4.7, 4.5, 4.4, 4.2, 3.9, 3.6],
    'reviews': [1204, 3410, 982, 457, 2216, 313]})

# Put the rank in each label so every label is unique
products['label'] = ['{}'.format(p)
                     for i, p in enumerate(products['product'])]

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# Horizontal bars sorted by rating
sns.barplot(data=products, x='rating', y='label', orient='h',
            color='#f4b400', ax=ax)

for i, row in products.iterrows():
    # Annotate the product name on its bar, left aligned at x = 0.1
    ax.text(0.1, i, row['product'],
            ha='left', va='center', size='x-small')

    # Label each bar with the rating and the review count
    ax.text(row['rating'] * .65, i,
            '{:.1f} \u2605 ({:,})'.format(row['rating'], row['reviews']),
            va='center', size='xx-small')

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('TrailMix Pro Tops Customer Ratings')
ax.set_xlabel('Average Rating (out of 5)')
ax.set_ylabel('')
ax.set_xlim(0, 6.2)
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 6))

# Remove the y-axis labels since the names are on the bars
ax.set_yticks([])
sns.despine(left=True)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 3: Board Game Leader Board

Gold, silver, and bronze colors make the podium obvious without a legend. The data are fictional.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rank-game
#| fig-cap: "A leader board of fictional board game scores. The top three players are colored gold, silver, and bronze."

# Fictional final scores, highest first
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    'player': ['Maya', 'Jonas', 'Priya', 'Theo', 'Lena', 'Omar'],

    ax.text(row['points'] + 1, i, str(row['points']),
            va='center', size='small')

ax.set_title('{} Wins With {} Points'.format(
    scores['player'][0], scores['points'][0]))
ax.set_xlabel('Final Score')
ax.set_ylabel('')
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)

ax.set_yticks([])

plt.show()
```

Rank by efficiency rather than by size. The best performer gets a highlight color and the rest share a muted one.

## Candidate 5: Lollipop Chart

A lollipop chart carries the same information as a bar chart with far less ink, which helps when the list is long.


## Candidate 6: Bump Chart

A bump chart shows how a ranking changes over time, so it tells a story about winners and losers rather than a single snapshot.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rank-bump
#| fig-cap: "A bump chart ranks six countries by life expectancy at the start of each decade from 1970 to 2020. Rank 1 is the highest life expectancy."

# Load the health expenditure dataset
health = sns.load_dataset('healthexp')

# Reshape to one column per country and fill in any missing years
wide = health.pivot(index='Year', columns='Country', values='Life_Expectancy')
wide = wide.reindex(range(1970, 2021)).interpolate(limit_direction='both')

# Rank the countries at the start of each decade (1 = highest)
years = [1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020]
ranks = wide.loc[years].rank(axis=1, ascending=False)

# Assign one color to each country
palette = dict(zip(ranks.columns, sns.color_palette('tab10', len(ranks.columns))))

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))

# One line per country, labeled at the right end
for country in ranks.columns:
    ax.plot(ranks.index, ranks[country], marker='o', linewidth=3,
            color=palette[country])
    ax.text(2021.5, ranks.loc[2020, country], country,
            color=palette[country], va='center', size='x-small')

# Put rank 1 at the top
ax.invert_yaxis()

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Japan Rose To #1 While The USA Fell To Last')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Rank (1 = Highest)')
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_yticks(range(1, 7))
ax.set_xlim(1968, 2032)
sns.despine()

plt.show()
```

# The Process Or Status Stories

A process or status story answers *where are we right now?* It reports the current state of a procedure, a measurement, or a flow against a goal. Dials, meters, progress bars, and flow diagrams all do this job. Seaborn has no built-in status graphics, so these examples use Matplotlib shapes. All of the values are fictional.

Candidates: @fig-status-gauge, @fig-status-speedometer, @fig-status-battery, @fig-status-progress, @fig-status-bullet, @fig-status-admissions-sankey, @fig-status-recruiting-sankey.

```{python}
#| label: status-data

# Import the Matplotlib shapes used to draw the dials and meters
from matplotlib.patches import Wedge, Rectangle, Circle

# Load the Titanic dataset for the Sankey diagram
titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
```

## Candidate 1: Gauge

A half-donut gauge shows a single percentage against a goal. It is simple, familiar, and needs no explanation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-status-gauge
#| fig-cap: "A half-donut gauge showing that 78% of deliveries were on time. The filled arc is the current value and the gray arc is the remainder."

# A fictional on-time delivery rate
value = 78

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))

# Half donut: value, remainder, and an invisible lower half
ax.pie([value, 100 - value, 100], colors=['seagreen', 'lightgray', 'none'],
       startangle=180, counterclock=False,
       wedgeprops={'width': 0.3, 'edgecolor': 'none'})

# Print the value in the middle of the arc
ax.text(0, 0.1, '{}%'.format(value), ha='center', va='center', size='xx-large')

# Show only the top half
ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.1)

# Set the title
ax.set_title('On-Time Delivery Rate')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 2: Speedometer

A needle on a dial with colored zones shows not only the current value but also whether it is in a safe range.

```{python}
#| label: fig-status-speedometer
#| fig-cap: "A speedometer with green, yellow, and red zones and a needle pointing to the current speed of 62 mph."

# A fictional current speed and the top of the dial
speed = 62
top_speed = 120

# Colored zones as (start, end, color)
zones = [(0, 60, '#a8e6a1'), (60, 90, '#ffe08a'), (90, 120, '#f4a6a6')]

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))

# Draw each zone as a ring segment (180 degrees is zero, 0 degrees is top speed)
for start, end, color in zones:
    ax.add_patch(Wedge((0, 0), 1, 180 - 180 * end / top_speed,
                       180 - 180 * start / top_speed, width=0.3,
                       facecolor=color, edgecolor='white'))

# Number the dial every 20 mph
for v in range(0, top_speed + 1, 20):
    angle = np.radians(180 - 180 * v / top_speed)
    ax.text(1.15 * np.cos(angle), 1.15 * np.sin(angle), str(v),
            ha='center', va='center', size='x-small')

# Draw the needle and its hub
angle = np.radians(180 - 180 * speed / top_speed)
ax.plot([0, 0.85 * np.cos(angle)], [0, 0.85 * np.sin(angle)],
        color='black', linewidth=3)
ax.add_patch(Circle((0, 0), 0.06, color='black'))

# Print the current value below the hub
ax.text(0, -0.3, '{} mph'.format(speed), ha='center', size='x-large')

# Tidy the axes
ax.set_xlim(-1.35, 1.35)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.3)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.axis('off')

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 5: Bullet Chart

A bullet chart compares the current value (the black bar) to a target (the red line) and to qualitative ranges (the gray bands). Showing every metric as a percent of target lets one chart hold several measures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-status-bullet
#| fig-cap: "A bullet chart of three fictional business metrics. The black bar is the current value as a percent of target, the red line is the target, and the gray bands mark poor, fair, and good ranges."

# Fictional metrics as a percent of their target
metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    'metric': ['Revenue', 'New Customers', 'Satisfaction'],
    'pct_of_target': [92, 108, 74]})

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.25))

for i, v in enumerate(metrics['pct_of_target']):
    # Qualitative ranges: poor, fair, and good
    ax.barh(i, 120, height=0.7, color='#eeeeee')
    ax.barh(i, 90, height=0.7, color='#d9d9d9')
    ax.barh(i, 60, height=0.7, color='#bdbdbd')

    # Current value and target line
    ax.barh(i, v, height=0.25, color='black')
    ax.plot([100, 100], [i - 0.3, i + 0.3], color='red', linewidth=3)

    # Label the value
    ax.text(122, i, '{}%'.format(v), va='center', size='small')

# Label the rows
ax.set_yticks(range(len(metrics)))
ax.set_yticklabels(metrics['metric'])
ax.invert_yaxis()

# Set the title and axis labels
ax.set_title('Satisfaction Lags Its Target')
ax.set_xlabel('Percent of Target')
ax.set_xlim(0, 135)
ax.set_xticks([0, 50, 100])
sns.despine(left=True)

plt.show()
```

## Candidate 6: Sankey Diagram Of A Process

A Sankey diagram follows a cohort through a sequence of stages, with time running left to right. The thickness of each ribbon is the number of people who took that path, so the audience sees both where people come from and where they are lost along the way. Matplotlib has no full-featured Sankey function, so this one is drawn with a short helper. The data are fictional.

```{python}
#| label: fig-status-admissions-sankey
#| fig-cap: "A Sankey diagram follows a fictional cohort of 2,000 prospective students from the source of their inquiry, through a campus visit, application, admission decision, and enrollment. The thickness of each ribbon is the number of students."

# Import the shape used to draw the nodes
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

# The stages of the process, in time order
stages = ['Source', 'Campus Visit', 'Application',
          'Decision', 'Enrollment']

# The categories shown within each stage, top to bottom
order = [['Social Media', 'College Fairs', 'Mailings', 'Referrals'],
         ['Visited', 'Did Not Visit'],
         ['Applied', 'Did Not Apply'],
         ['Accepted', 'Waitlisted', 'Denied'],
         ['Enrolled', 'Did Not Enroll']]

# Fictional flows: students moving from a category in one stage
# (stage = 0 is Source) to a category in the next stage
flows = pd.DataFrame([
    (0, 'Social Media', 'Visited', 240),
    (0, 'Social Media', 'Did Not Visit', 560),
    (0, 'College Fairs', 'Visited', 220),
    (0, 'College Fairs', 'Did Not Visit', 280),
    (0, 'Mailings', 'Visited', 140),
    (0, 'Mailings', 'Did Not Visit', 260),
    (0, 'Referrals', 'Visited', 180),
    (0, 'Referrals', 'Did Not Visit', 120),
    (1, 'Visited', 'Applied', 560),
    (1, 'Visited', 'Did Not Apply', 220),
    (1, 'Did Not Visit', 'Applied', 440),
    (1, 'Did Not Visit', 'Did Not Apply', 780),
    (2, 'Applied', 'Accepted', 400),
    (2, 'Applied', 'Waitlisted', 300),
    (2, 'Applied', 'Denied', 300),
    (3, 'Accepted', 'Enrolled', 240),
    (3, 'Accepted', 'Did Not Enroll', 160),
    (3, 'Waitlisted', 'Enrolled', 60),
    (3, 'Waitlisted', 'Did Not Enroll', 240)],
    columns=['stage', 'source', 'target', 'n'])

# Colors: one per source, then green for success, orange for waiting, gray for exits
palette = dict(zip(order[0], sns.color_palette('Set2', 4)))
palette.update({'Visited': '#6baed6', 'Did Not Visit': 'lightgray',
                'Applied': '#6baed6', 'Did Not Apply': 'lightgray',
                'Accepted': '#74c476', 'Waitlisted': '#fdae6b',
                'Denied': 'lightgray', 'Enrolled': '#74c476',
                'Did Not Enroll': 'lightgray'})

# Helper that draws the nodes and the ribbons between them
def draw_flow(ax, flows, stages, order, palette, width=0.1):
    # Each node is as tall as the larger of what flows in and what flows out
    size = {}
    for s in range(len(stages)):
        for cat in order[s]:
            inflow = flows.loc[(flows['stage'] == s - 1) &
                               (flows['target'] == cat), 'n'].sum()
            outflow = flows.loc[(flows['stage'] == s) &
                                (flows['source'] == cat), 'n'].sum()
            size[(s, cat)] = max(inflow, outflow)

    # Stack the nodes in each stage, centered vertically
    gap = 0.03 * sum(size[(0, cat)] for cat in order[0])
    heights = [sum(size[(s, cat)] for cat in order[s]) + gap * (len(order[s]) - 1)
               for s in range(len(stages))]
    pos = {}
    for s in range(len(stages)):
        y = (max(heights) - heights[s]) / 2
        for cat in order[s]:
            pos[(s, cat)] = y
            y += size[(s, cat)] + gap

    # Track how much of each node the ribbons have used so far
    out_used, in_used = dict(pos), dict(pos)
    t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
    smooth = t * t * (3 - 2 * t)

    # Draw one ribbon per flow
    for row in flows.itertuples():
        s = row.stage
        y0 = out_used[(s, row.source)]
        y1 = in_used[(s + 1, row.target)]
        out_used[(s, row.source)] += row.n
        in_used[(s + 1, row.target)] += row.n
        bottom = y0 + (y1 - y0) * smooth
        ax.fill_between(s + width + (1 - width) * t, bottom, bottom + row.n,
                        color=palette[row.source], alpha=0.5, linewidth=0)

    # Draw the nodes and label them with the category and count
    last = len(stages) - 1
    for s in range(len(stages)):
        for cat in order[s]:
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((s, pos[(s, cat)]), width, size[(s, cat)],
                                   color=palette[cat]))
            if s == 0:
                x, ha = s - 0.03, 'right'
            elif s == last:
                x, ha = s + width + 0.03, 'left'
            else:
                x, ha = s + width / 2, 'center'
            ax.text(x, pos[(s, cat)] + size[(s, cat)] / 2,
                    '{}\n{:,}'.format(cat, size[(s, cat)]),
                    ha=ha, va='center', size=7,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.7))

    # Name each stage along the bottom, rotated to fit
    ax.set_xticks([s + width / 2 for s in range(len(stages))])
    ax.set_xticklabels(stages, size='x-small', rotation=45, ha='right')
    ax.set_xlim(-1.4, last + width + 1.4)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.invert_yaxis()

# Compute the share of prospects who enroll
enrolled = flows.loc[(flows['stage'] == 3) & (flows['target'] == 'Enrolled'), 'n'].sum()
prospects = flows.loc[flows['stage'] == 0, 'n'].sum()

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))

# Draw the diagram
draw_flow(ax, flows, stages, order, palette)

# Set the title
ax.set_title('Prospective College Student Journey')
sns.despine(left=True, bottom=True)

plt.show()
```

# Outtakes

## Candidate 1: Sankey Diagram

A Sankey diagram shows how a population flows through the stages of a process. The thickness of each ribbon is the number of people (or items) that took that path. Matplotlib has no full-featured Sankey function, so this one is drawn with a short helper.

```{python}
#| label: fig-status-sankey
#| fig-cap: "A Sankey diagram follows Titanic passengers from passenger class, to sex, to whether they survived. The thickness of each ribbon is the number of passengers."

# Build a table of the three stages in the flow
flow = pd.DataFrame({
    'Class': titanic['class'].astype(str),
    'Sex': titanic['sex'].str.title(),
    'Outcome': titanic['alive'].map({'yes': 'Survived', 'no': 'Did Not Survive'})})

# The stages (in order) and the categories to show within each stage
stages = ['Class', 'Sex', 'Outcome']
order = {'Class': ['First', 'Second', 'Third'],
         'Sex': ['Female', 'Male'],
         'Outcome': ['Survived', 'Did Not Survive']}

# One color for every category
palette = dict(zip(
    ['First', 'Second', 'Third', 'Female', 'Male', 'Survived', 'Did Not Survive'],
    sns.color_palette('Set2', 7)))

# Helper that draws the nodes and the ribbons between them
def draw_sankey(ax, df, stages, order, palette, width=0.12):
    gap = 0.04 * len(df)

    # Stack the nodes in each stage and remember where each one sits
    pos, size = {}, {}
    for stage in stages:
        y = 0
        for cat in order[stage]:
            pos[(stage, cat)] = y
            size[(stage, cat)] = (df[stage] == cat).sum()
            y += size[(stage, cat)] + gap

    # Track how much of each node has been used by ribbons so far
    out_used = dict(pos)
    in_used = dict(pos)

    # Draw the ribbons between each pair of neighboring stages
    for i in range(len(stages) - 1):
        a, b = stages[i], stages[i + 1]
        for ca in order[a]:
            for cb in order[b]:
                n = ((df[a] == ca) & (df[b] == cb)).sum()
                if n == 0:
                    continue
                y0, y1 = out_used[(a, ca)], in_used[(b, cb)]
                out_used[(a, ca)] += n
                in_used[(b, cb)] += n
                t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
                s = t * t * (3 - 2 * t)
                bottom = y0 + (y1 - y0) * s
                ax.fill_between(i + width + (1 - width) * t,
                                bottom, bottom + n,
                                color=palette[ca], alpha=0.5, linewidth=0)

    # Draw the nodes and label them with the category and count
    for i, stage in enumerate(stages):
        for cat in order[stage]:
            key = (stage, cat)
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i, pos[key]), width, size[key],
                                   color=palette[cat]))
            ax.text(i + width / 2, pos[key] + size[key] / 2,
                    '{}\n{}'.format(cat, size[key]),
                    ha='center', va='center', size='xx-small',
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.8))

    # Name each stage along the bottom
    ax.set_xticks([i + width / 2 for i in range(len(stages))])
    ax.set_xticklabels(stages)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, len(stages) - 1 + width + 0.1)
    ax.set_yticks([])

# Create a figure and axis object
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

# Draw the diagram
draw_sankey(ax, flow, stages, order, palette)

# Set the title
ax.set_title('Survival Depended On Class And Sex')
sns.despine(left=True, bottom=True)

plt.show()
```
